Artificial intelligence is being sold to the public as the next great technological revolution, promising unprecedented productivity, scientific breakthroughs, and solutions to some of humanity's most difficult problems. But who benefits from this transformation, who pays its costs, and who gets to decide how the technology is deployed? Those questions drove a panel titled “AI Is Coming for You, But You Can Fight Back” at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at California State University, Los Angeles. articles.title: Workers Can Govern, but They Need Power First
articles.author: Jared Abbott
articles.content_excerpt: According to data from a sweeping new study of working-class legislators by political scientists Nicholas Carnes and Noam Lupu, only about 2 percent of legislators across the world’s democracies held a working-class job — which the authors define as manual, service, or clerical work — before getting into politics. Yet as the authors document in their new book , Keeping Workers Off the Ballot: How Democracy Undermines Working-Class Representation , about seven in ten jobs in a typical democracy are working-class jobs, from construction workers and truck drivers to servers, cashiers, receptionists, data-entry clerks, day laborers, and street vendors. articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. There’s a kerfuffle about art being political, with journalists and writers I respect, such as Matt Taibbi and Caitlin Johnstone , coming down on opposite sides of the issue. Johnstone puts it bluntly : “I have no respect for this idea that art is somehow separable from politics. articles.title: Exploring the Mirror World of the Chinese Internet
articles.author: Yi-Ling Liu
articles.content_excerpt: China’s internet is known for a vast system of censorship and surveillance that has evolved alongside its booming digital economy. Yet the story of the Chinese internet is not simply one of authoritarian control or unrestricted growth. In her book , The Wall Dancers: Searching for Freedom and Connection on the Chinese Internet , journalist and author Yi-Ling Liu explores how people navigate within the constantly shifting boundaries of censorship, carving out creative spaces for communities and political expression. Lawson, Jr. on his birthday reminded me that this latter-day prophet often invited us to use his term, “plantation capitalism,” to describe how things really work in the U.S. economy. articles.title: The Left Needs an Answer to the Center’s New Cold War Program
articles.author: Caleb Brennan
articles.content_excerpt: Between the Israeli genocide in Gaza and the calamitous stalemate of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, the American foreign policy consensus has been coming apart. Popular support for the United States’ violent foreign policy has reached an unprecedented nadir , as Americans increasingly recognize the downsides of maintaining a global empire. In particular, US military largesse has come at the cost of spending on domestic needs , and voters are increasingly unhappy about this trade-off. According to polling by ReThink Media and the Costs of War Project at Brown University, 59 percent of respondents found the Trump administration’s proposed 2027 Pentagon budget of $1.5 trillion to be excessive. articles.author: Ethan Rooney
articles.content_excerpt: Britain’s latest prime minister, Andy Burnham, raised hackles on his first trip to the North of Ireland when he declared a referendum on Irish unity to be “off the table.” Burnham may simply have intended to say that it wasn’t on the short-term agenda, since there is no sign as yet that a majority of people in the North would vote for a united Ireland. But his choice of words implied that it was for the British government to decide whether a referendum should happen, which angered nationalists. Burnham’s secretary of state for Northern Ireland, Chris Bryant, made another clumsy intervention when the unionist Orange Order tried to march down the nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown. articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content_excerpt: “The smarter our life, the less control we have over it.” —Jathan Sadowski [1] In a world where Big Tech too often sets the terms and conditions of basic human interaction within and beyond the workplace, more and more people are wondering how many of the supposedly “necessary” or “inevitable” algorithmic technologies we really need. Is it even possible for this digital machinery to serve the long-term interests of the many instead of the short-term interests of the few? For French Marxist philosopher and first-wave eco-socialist André Gorz, the answer, in many cases, was no. “It is only because capital needs consumers for its products that production also serves human needs,” he wrote. articles.author: Sharon Kyle

The Civil War ended slavery, but it did not end the ideas that made slavery possible. That distinction, according to civil rights attorney Bryan Stevenson, helps explain why racial injustice has remained a permanent fixture in American institutions long after the abolition of slavery, the end of Jim Crow, and the victories of the civil rights movement. Speaking with California Governor Gavin Newsom in Montgomery, Alabama, Stevenson offered an analysis of American history that challenges conventional accounts of racial progress. articles.title: Palestinians Face Down the Israeli Genocid
articles.author: Ramzy Baroud, Robert Corsini, Dick Price, Sharon Kyle
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On October 3, 2026, Palestinian American journalist, author, and historian Ramzy Baroud delivered a powerful keynote address at the Fourth Annual Left Coast Forum at California State University, Los Angeles. Speaking about Israel's genocide in Gaza and the Palestinian struggle for liberation, Baroud combined family history, anti-colonial analysis, and an urgent call for international solidarity. His central message was unmistakable: Palestinians are not simply victims of history. They are active participants in shaping it, and their refusal to disappear represents a fundamental challenge to the colonial system seeking to displace them. Ramzy Baroud: Left Coast Forum (49:29)

articles.title: Economics News for Workers, October 2026
articles.content_excerpt: On September 16, the Federal Reserve Board raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percent, the first rate hike in three years. Minutes from the meeting which were released in early October indicate that the board of governors expects to impose another rate increase before the end of the year. They meet again on October 28 and December 9. The rate increase, while justified as a means to fight inflation, was primarily meant to reassure international financial markets that the U.S. will make good on its debt, which has spiraled due to the combination of tax cuts for the wealthy and military spending. articles.title: Dattner’s Architects Say They Want a Union
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content_excerpt: On the west side of Manhattan, near the entrance to the Holland Tunnel, there is a nearly seventy-foot-tall concrete building containing five thousand tons of road salt. The walls of the Spring Street Salt Shed slope inward and outward in enormous pale planes; the whole thing is meant to resemble a grain of salt. Across the street stands a much larger garage that accommodates more than 150 sanitation vehicles, its long facades covered in glass and aluminum louvers. The two buildings were designed together, an attempt to make a sprawling sanitation facility fit into a residential neighborhood where residents had initially fought its construction. articles.title: More Than Ball Fields
articles.author: Bill Gould
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For generations of Altadena families, Charles S. Farnsworth Park has been much more than ballfields at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains. It has been one of the places where Altadena comes together. Children learned to throw and catch there, parents watched from the stands, coaches became mentors and neighbors became friends. But Farnsworth has always served a broader community. Its playgrounds, tennis and pickleball courts and basketball courts provided recreation for all ages.
